terms.gloss: declension; any inflection of a word
terms.comment: In Varro and Quintilian every change of form, of nouns and of verbs alike; the later grammarians kept it for nouns (Lewis & Short). To decline a noun is nōmen dēclīnāre (Quint. 1.4.22; Traupman 246); the first declension, prīma dēclīnātiō (Traupman 222).

phrases.latin: nōmina dēclīnāre et verba in prīmīs puerī sciant, neque enim aliter pervenīre ad intellēctum sequentium possunt
phrases.english: above all, let boys know how to decline nouns and verbs, for they cannot otherwise come to understand what follows

phrases.latin: comparātiō in nōminibus aut genus dēprehendit aut dēclīnātiōnem; … dēclīnātiōnem, ut sī veniat in dubium, hāc domū dīcendum sit an hāc domō et domuum an domōrum
phrases.english: in nouns, comparison settles either the gender or the declension: the declension, when it is doubtful whether to say hāc domū or hāc domō, domuum or domōrum

phrases.latin: Dā dēclīnātiōnem nōminis, generis fēminīnī, numerī singulāris.
phrases.english: Give the declension of a noun of the feminine gender, singular number.

sources: Lewis & Short: declinatio · Lewis & Short: declino
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. declension.
